verses.text: After traveling through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they arrived in Thessalonica, where there was a Jewish synagogue.
As usual, Paul went in and spent three Sabbaths discussing the Scriptures with them.
He explained and showed them that the Messiah had to suffer and rise from the dead. “This Jesus I’m telling you about,” he said, “is the Messiah.”
Some were convinced and joined Paul and Silas, along with a large number of devout Greeks and quite a few leading women.

But the Jews who refused to believe recruited some troublemakers from the marketplace, stirred up a crowd, and threw the city into chaos. They attacked Jason’s house, looking for Paul and Silas so they could drag them before the people.
When they couldn’t find them, they dragged Jason and some other believers before the city officials, shouting, “These people who have turned the whole world upside down have come here too!
“Jason welcomed them into his home. They’re all defying Caesar’s decrees, claiming there’s another king named Jesus!”
The crowd and city officials were alarmed when they heard this.
After taking bail from Jason and the others, they let them go.
That very night, the believers sent Paul and Silas to Berea. When they arrived, they went to the Jewish synagogue.
The Bereans were more open-minded than the Thessalonians. They eagerly welcomed the message and checked the Scriptures every day to see if Paul’s words were true.
Many of them believed, including quite a few prominent Greek women and men.
But when the Jews in Thessalonica heard Paul was preaching God’s message in Berea too, they came there and stirred up trouble with the crowds.
The believers quickly sent Paul toward the coast, while Silas and Timothy stayed behind.
The people escorting Paul took him all the way to Athens. Then they left with instructions for Silas and Timothy to join him as soon as possible.
While Paul waited for them in Athens, he was deeply disturbed by a city full of idols.
So he reasoned with Jews and devout people in the synagogue, and every day he talked in the marketplace with whoever happened to be there.

Some Epicurean and Stoic philosophers got into discussions with him. A few asked, “What is this chatterbox trying to say?” Others said, “He seems to be promoting foreign gods,” because Paul was announcing Jesus and the resurrection.
They took him to the Areopagus and said, “Can we hear more about this new teaching you’re sharing?
“You’re bringing some strange ideas to our ears. We want to understand what they mean.”
Now, the Athenians and foreigners living there spent most of their time telling or hearing about the latest thing.
Paul stood in the middle of the Areopagus and said, “People of Athens, I can see you take your worship very seriously.
“As I walked around and looked at the things you worship, I even found an altar inscribed, ‘TO AN UNKNOWN GOD.’ What you worship without knowing—I’m here to tell you about.
“The God who made the world and everything in it is Lord of heaven and earth. He doesn’t live in temples built by human hands.
“He doesn’t need people to serve him as if he lacked anything. He himself gives everyone life, breath, and everything else.
“From one ancestor, he made every nation to live across the whole earth. He set their appointed times and the boundaries of where they live,
“so they would reach out for God and perhaps find him. But he isn’t far from any of us.
“As some of your own poets have said, ‘In him we live, move, and exist,’ and ‘We are his children too.’
“So if we are God’s children, we shouldn’t imagine that God is like gold, silver, or stone shaped by human skill and ideas.
“God overlooked the times when people didn’t know better. But now he commands everyone everywhere to turn back to him,
“because he has set a day to judge the world fairly through the man he appointed. He proved this to everyone by raising him from the dead.”
When they heard about resurrection from the dead, some laughed at him. Others said, “We want to hear you speak about this again.”
Then Paul left the gathering.
But some people joined him and believed, including Dionysius, a member of the Areopagus council, a woman named Damaris, and others.
